slides.title: The Bootstrap
slides.subtitle: How sure can I be about a number from one sample?
slides.hook: you have 40 cells. you want the uncertainty of their mean.

slides.q: You resample your 40 cells with replacement, many times. What happens to the spread of the means if you had 160 cells instead?
slides.why: The spread of a mean falls with the **square root** of n. 4x more cells gives sqrt(4) = 2x less spread. Keep this number. The simulation later shows it.

notes.t: The **population** is every cell you could measure. Your **sample** is the 40 you did measure.
How much single cells differ from each other. More cells do not make it smaller.
How much the **mean** would change if you repeated the study. More cells make it smaller.

slides.title: Works vs. fails

a.t:
- Means, medians, regression slopes
- n is moderate or large
- Values are **independent**

b.t:
- Extremes (max, min)
- Very small n (under ~15)
- Cells from the same patient treated as independent

slides.hand: spatial omics trap: resample patients, not cells

cards.q: The 95% CI is 48.9 to 55.1. Is there a 95% chance the true mean is inside it?
cards.a: Not in the usual (frequentist) reading. The **method** catches the true mean in 95% of studies. This one interval either contains it or not.

cards.q: You bootstrap the **largest** cell area. What goes wrong?
cards.a: A resample can never beat the sample's maximum. The interval is too narrow and sits too low.

cards.q: 3 patients, 10,000 cells each. What is n for the bootstrap?
cards.a: n = 3. Resample **patients**, not cells. Cells from one patient are not independent (**pseudoreplication**).

cards.q: SD or SE: which one shrinks when you measure more cells?
cards.a: SE. SD is the spread of cells and stays about the same. SE = SD / √n is the uncertainty of the mean.

cards.q: You have 12 tissue sections from 4 mice. What do you resample?
cards.a: The **4 mice**. Sections from one mouse share biology, so they are not independent.

cards.q: Your marker gene is detected in 30% of cells. How do you get an interval for that 30%?
cards.a: Resample **samples or donors** with replacement, recompute the share each time, and read the spread.

cards.q: A classifier scores 0.91 AUC on one test set. How unsure is that number?
cards.a: Resample the **test set** with replacement, recompute AUC each time. The spread is its uncertainty.
Without replacement, each resample is the same set of values. The statistic never changes, so you see no spread.

cards.q: More resamples (B) makes the interval narrower. True?
cards.a: No. B only makes the estimate of the interval more stable. Only more data (n) makes it narrower.

cards.q: Why must each resample have the same size n as your sample?
cards.a: The SE depends on n. Smaller resamples spread more and would overstate the uncertainty.

slides.title: Take it with you
points: The bootstrap estimates uncertainty from **one** sample.
Resample with replacement, recalculate, repeat B times.
The spread of results is the standard error.
It cannot fix a sample that does not represent the population.
slides.caveat: Resample at the level of independent units (patient, slide, mouse), not at the level of cells or spots.
